beats.narration_text: Vanakkam — this is Liam, in for Bear. A student, Saloni, pitched her Computational Skepticism final project: a Job Application Priority Checker. I asked Claude what Professor Bear would tell her. Short version — make the skepticism load-bearing, not decorative.

props.command: What feedback would Professor Bear give Saloni on her Computational Skepticism final project — a "Job Application Priority Checker"?
output: name the target, gate work authorization, and let it break.

beats.narration_text: First, why a good pitch is dangerous.

The pitch is reasonable and on-theme: build a recommender that explains itself. That's the trap. It's reasonable in a way that lets you stop at 'it explains itself' without ever hitting the hard problems the course exists to teach.
beats.show: A tidy 'recommender that explains itself' card sits looking finished — then a crack runs through it.

props.question: A recommender that explains itself — where does the trap hide?
props.commit: It stops at 'explains itself' without hitting the hard problems the course exists to teach

beats.narration_text: Three things make it harder than it looks. Work authorization isn't a neutral feature. Transparent and correct are different properties. And it overlaps Bear's own Reallocation Engine — so he knows exactly where this class of project fails.
beats.show: Three labels resolve in turn on the stage: work-auth · transparent≠correct · Bear's own turf.

beats.narration_text: Start where every ranking has to start.

A ranking is a claim: jobs higher up are better bets. Better by what — interview odds? An offer? Sponsorship that actually follows through? Salary? Time-to-hire? Each target produces a different ranking. A recommendation that won't name its target isn't transparent — it's just legible.
beats.show: One list fans into five differently-ordered lists, one per target, as the words land.

beats.narration_text: Because until Saloni writes the outcome variable down — before a line of ranking logic — the transparency she's planning is cosmetic. Legible math pointed at an unnamed goal is still a black box.
beats.show: A student at a screen full of job cards, no clear 'best' — slow push in.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a person facing a wall of unranked job cards, documentary duotone.

beats.narration_text: So the honest first version isn't an ML model with an explainability layer bolted on. Ask for this:

props.command: Write an explicit, inspectable priority_score — user-adjustable weights, each factor normalized 0–1, returns the sub-scores as the explanation.

beats.narration_text: An explicit weighted score. Skills, experience, location, sponsorship — each weight visible and adjustable. And it returns the sub-scores alongside the number. That dictionary is the explanation.
beats.show: Onda code-block types out priority_score(...) — weights line, then the returned sub-score dict highlighted.

props.title: priority_score.py
props.code:
def priority_score(job, profile, weights):
    skill_match     = jaccard(job.required_skills, profile.skills)
    experience_fit  = min(profile.years_exp / job.years_required, 1.0)
    location_fit    = 1.0 if job.location in profile.preferred else 0.3
    sponsorship_fit = sponsorship_compatibility(job, profile)
    score = (
        weights['skills']      * skill_match
      + weights['experience']  * experience_fit
      + weights['location']    * location_fit
      + weights['sponsorship'] * sponsorship_fit
    )
    return score, {
        'skill_match':      skill_match,
        'experience_fit':   experience_fit,
        'location_fit':     location_fit,
        'sponsorship_fit':  sponsorship_fit,
    }

beats.narration_text: This beats a black box with SHAP on top, because the reasoning IS the mechanism — not a post-hoc approximation of a mechanism you can't see. Show the work by making the work simple enough to show.
beats.show: Two paths race: a transparent gearbox vs a black box trailing a dotted 'explanation' guess; the gearbox lands first.

beats.narration_text: Now the variable that breaks everything.

Work authorization is not a preference like location. It's a hard eligibility gate with legal consequences. A job that won't sponsor isn't 'seventy percent as good' for an F-1 student whose OPT is running out — it's disqualifying. Blend it into a weighted average and you can top-rank a job she literally cannot take.
beats.show: A smooth score bar for 'sponsorship' snaps into a hard 0/1 cliff; a blended average floats a red job to #1.

beats.narration_text: And it's time-bounded. OPT, CPT, STEM OPT windows change what 'good fit' even means over a single job search…
beats.show: A visa/OPT countdown clock, hands moving; camera holds on the shrinking runway.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a calendar/clock motif for an eligibility window; continuity into B10 (vox_run R1).

beats.narration_text: So the fix is a gate function that carries its own doubt. Ask for this:

props.command: Model sponsorship as a hard 0/1 gate plus a data-confidence flag (confirmed vs inferred from USCIS filings) — not a smoothed score that hides the cliff.

beats.narration_text: A hard zero-or-one, not a penalty — and a confidence flag on the data behind it. 'Confirmed' is not the same as 'inferred from a public dataset with a one-year lag.' The flag matters more than it looks.
beats.show: Onda code-block types sponsorship_compatibility(...); the `confidence` line highlights terracotta.

props.title: sponsorship_compatibility.py

beats.narration_text: Employer sponsorship history is a noisy proxy — three visas last year, zero this year isn't the same signal. Honest visualization means showing that doubt, not collapsing it into one clean bar. Grade the source before you trust it.
beats.show: A 'confirmed' bar sits solid; an 'inferred' bar redraws as hatched/uncertain with a one-year-lag tag.

beats.narration_text: Robustness isn't a checkbox.

'I'll do robustness testing' is easy to fake — nudge an input, watch the score wiggle, call it done. The useful test asks whether small, realistic changes flip the recommendation. If a ten-percent change in self-reported skill match reorders her top three, the ranking was a statistical tie wearing false confidence.
beats.show: Top-3 rows sit stable; a ±10% nudge on skill match swaps ranks 1 and 3 as the words land.

beats.narration_text: Four tests worth requiring, in writing, not just code. Near-threshold: does a small change flip the top pick? Missing data: does a blank field silently tank a good match? Adversarial: can she inflate her own skill self-rating to game it? Distribution shift: does a scheme tuned on software roles misrank a hardware or research job?
beats.show: Four test chips resolve: Near-threshold · Missing data · Adversarial · Distribution shift.

beats.narration_text: The honest move on a blank field is to surface 'insufficient data,' not default it to zero or the mean — both quietly bias the result. And a tool that trusts self-reported skills uncritically doesn't have transparency; it has a gap where the most obvious failure walks in.
beats.show: A form with a blank field; a terracotta ring draws on around an 'insufficient data' tag instead of a silent 0.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a partly-filled form; ring annotation added at previz.

beats.narration_text: Where tools like this usually lie.
The classic failure is a single composite score shown as if it were measured. Bucket it — strong, moderate, weak — with the sub-scores visible. Less precise, more honest.
beats.show: A crisp percentage dissolves into a 'Strong' bucket with the four sub-scores fanning out beneath.

beats.narration_text: So the visualization has to show the weights and the sub-scores, not just the output — a friendly number with a hidden recipe is still a black box. And shade the uncertainty on sponsorship specifically: tag any unconfirmed job 'data quality: inferred.'
beats.show: A composite bar expands to reveal weight×sub-score components; the sponsorship component carries a hatched 'inferred' shade.

beats.narration_text: The through-line under all five.

Every part points at one idea: transparent and correct are different properties. A tool can expose all its reasoning and still reason badly. The two highest-leverage moves — grade your sources, and separate the hard eligibility gate from the soft preference score — are exactly what Bear's Reallocation Engine already does. Point Saloni at those as open questions; don't hand her the solved version. The wrestling is the assignment.
beats.show: A 'transparent' pane and a 'correct' pane separate; a bridge labeled 'grade sources · split the gate' connects them.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Bear's notes for Saloni, in five: name the outcome variable before any ranking logic. Make work authorization a hard gate with a data-confidence flag, never a blended score. Test whether small, realistic changes flip the top pick. Show the weights and bucket the score instead of faking a decimal. And remember the through-line — transparent isn't correct. Strong topic. Now make the skepticism load-bearing.

artifactLines: Name the target before the ranking logic
Work authorization = hard gate + confidence flag, not a score
Robustness = does a small, realistic change flip the top pick
Show weights, bucket the score, shade the uncertainty
Transparent ≠ correct — grade sources, split gate from preference

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the reviewer's prompt Bear would use — paste it into Claude on any decision-support project like Saloni's. It makes the student name the target, turn eligibility variables into gates with graded data, run three real robustness tests, show the weights, and it ends in open questions instead of a handed-over answer. Run it on your own project before you call it transparent — and watch whether it can survive being made to break.

props.command: You're reviewing a decision-support proposal for a Computational Skepticism course — a tool that ranks options and claims to be 'transparent' and 'explainable.' Write feedback that (1) forces the student to name the exact outcome variable the ranking optimizes for before any scoring logic; (2) flags any legally/eligibility-loaded variable that must be a hard gate with a confirmed-vs-inferred data-confidence flag, not blended into a weighted score; (3) requires three concrete robustness tests — near-threshold flip, missing-data behavior, adversarial input; (4) requires the visualization to show sub-scores and weights and avoid false precision; and (5) ends with one or two open questions, not a prescribed architecture. Tone: encouraging but exacting.
